input.headline: The flicker of the ceiling lights matches the national grid record at 11:44:09 UTC on 8 Nov 2026, about 2 seconds from the stated start of 11:44:07.
input.difference: About 2 s, which is within the tool's margin of error. In practice there is no difference.
findings: The scene is a dim indoor room lit by ceiling strip lights, with no windows or on-screen clock. The lights' flicker carried a strong signal from the mains electricity, with 79% of the clip usable. The audio hum was too weak to use, at 8% usable.

For November 2026 the only grid record available logs the frequency every 15 seconds, which is coarser than the usual one-per-second record. Searching an hour either side of the stated time, the best match starts at 11:44:09 UTC with a score of 0.961 (1.0 is a perfect match). The next-best match in that window scored 0.847.

Split-halves test: I matched each half of the clip separately. The first half points to a start of 11:44:08 and the second half to 11:44:10. They agree, which gives no sign of a cut or splice inside the excerpt.
Sharpness test: the score drops clearly as the start time is moved 10 to 60 seconds away from the match, so the match is precise.

Other-days test: the best matches on the three days either side scored at most 0.908, compared with 0.961 for 8 Nov. That lead is real but modest. That is expected with a 5-minute clip and a coarse grid record, and it is why my confidence is medium rather than high.

This supports the stated timing, but it does not say who recorded the video or what happened in it.
